fatal_errors: The hypothesis concerns ethanol oxidation on PtPdRhRuIrOs nanoparticles, whereas the target study concerns HER and HOR on epitaxial PtRuFeCoNi-family shells supported on Pd nanocubes.
The proposed strain-relieving annealing intervention does not reconstruct the target intervention of depositing approximately five atomic layers of a quinary alloy onto {100}-faceted Pd seeds.

The cited evidence establishes that IrOsPtPdRhRu can enable a 12-electron ethanol-oxidation process, but it does not support the claimed causal link between lattice-strain distributions and CO2 selectivity.

Annealing cannot isolate lattice strain unless composition, atomic ordering, surface segregation, particle size, facet exposure, and oxidation state are independently demonstrated to remain unchanged.
The falsification rule incorrectly treats failure to achieve a verified strain change as falsification; that outcome would instead make the experiment uninformative.
explanation: This is a testable alternative hypothesis responsive to the surface wording of the query, but it does not reconstruct the hidden target. The target identifies a metastable, random, approximately equiatomic PtRuFeCoNi shell on {100} Pd nanocubes, with HER/HOR behavior governed by composition-dependent hydrogen and hydroxyl adsorption, orbital hybridization, Fe-to-Ru electron transfer during HER, and Pt/Co/Ni involvement during HOR. Its relevant comparisons are Pt/C, nine related quinary shells, binary/ternary controls, composition variants, and Pd@IrRuFeCoNi under specified acidic and alkaline conditions. The generated proposal instead changes strain by annealing and predicts ethanol-product selectivity. Its product analysis and paired baseline could discriminate an annealing-associated effect, but not strain specifically without stronger structural and surface controls. Evidence E1 supports the existence of unusual 12-electron ethanol oxidation and general HEA site heterogeneity, not the Gaussian adsorption-energy model, the premise of high CO2 selectivity, or the predicted effect of strain relaxation.
